title: The Unmannerly Tiger
originalTitle: 은혜를 모르는 호랑이 · Eunhyereul moreuneun horangi
note: A new, shortened adaptation of a tale printed in a 1922 collection. The source calls the tiger “Mountain Uncle” and places him in Kang Wen, an older spelling of Gangwon.

rights.basis: Source edition published before 1929 and identified as public domain by Project Gutenberg.

artLabel: A striped tiger peers into a mirrored forest trap.
scenes: High in the mountains of Gangwon lived a great striped tiger. The villagers called him Mountain Uncle.
He boasted that no hunter could fool him. He knew every rope, every cage, every trail of leaves laid over a pit—or so he believed.
One autumn morning, Mountain Uncle rounded a rock and stopped. Another tiger stood directly in his path.
He twitched his tail. The stranger twitched too. He bared his teeth. The stranger did the same.
Mountain Uncle sprang—and crashed through a roof of branches into a deep trap. The fierce stranger had been his own face in a mirror.
A Buddhist monk heard him groaning. Because the monk tried to be kind to every living creature, he lowered a log into the pit.
The tiger climbed out, shook the dust from his coat, and bowed. “Thank you,” he said. “But I am terribly hungry, so now I must eat you.”
The monk protested. A tree rustled that such ingratitude was shameful. A rock agreed. Still the tiger crept closer.
At last a little toad offered to judge—but first, he said, he must inspect the trap. While the tiger hurried ahead, the monk ran safely home.
The toad slipped into a narrow crack and called out his decision: “A creature who answers kindness with cruelty has very bad manners indeed.”
Mountain Uncle clawed uselessly at the stone. The little toad remained safe inside, and told the story for many years: strength may be loud, but good sense knows when to hop aside.
